title: Activation slicing and fragmented KV routing — proposal
content:
Summary:

This note proposes an operational design for combining activation-slicing (temporal/sequence splits) with a fragmented KV cache layout to improve multi-GPU serving latency and throughput for long-context models. The goal is to preserve tight latency SLOs for interactive requests while retaining high utilization on large batch workloads. We focus on three coupled subsystems: (1) KV fragmentation and placement, (2) activation slicing and microbatch routing, and (3) NCCL collectives and fallback tuning.

Motivation / current pain points:
- Long sequences blow up KV memory usage on large models; naive full-replication wastes memory or forces expensive NCCL shuffles.
- Heavy tail of request lengths leads to unpredictable per-request latency when doing global all-gather KV for each token step.
- Heterogeneous fleets (different GPU memory and interconnects) mean one-size NCCL configs are suboptimal across nodes.
- Need a graceful degraded mode for noisy neighbors / transient network congestion.

Design goals (prioritized):
1) Maintain 95th percentile token latency within SLO for interactive routes (e.g., 50ms per token target).
2) Avoid full-replication of KV for very long contexts; enable serving contexts up to 1M tokens without OOM across fleet.
3) Keep throughput (tokens/s) high for large-batch offline/streaming jobs.
4) Allow per-customer or per-route placement policies (isolate privacy-sensitive tenants).

High-level approach:
- Fragment the KV cache into columnar fragments (by KV key ranges or layer groups) that can be individually placed across GPUs. Fragments are the unit of movement/replication.
- For long sequences we slice activations across the time dimension (activation-slicing): instead of stepping token-by-token globally, we process slices of L tokens locally where possible, apply local KV updates, and asynchronously reconcile remote fragments when necessary.
- Use hybrid NCCL strategies: local-ring collectives for same-rack GPUs + tree/IB-tree for cross-rack; fall back to pipeline-stitching without collectives when the network is degraded.

Fragmented KV model:
- Fragment definition: fragment = (layers: [l_start..l_end], kv_range: [r_start..r_end]). Typical fragments map to 4–16 consecutive layers or 1/8th of KV keyspace.
- Placement policy: fragments are placed with a 3-tier policy: primary (local GPU), cold-replicas (other GPUs in same rack), and cross-rack read-only replicas. Placement respects tenant isolation tags.
- Metadata service stores fragment manifest keyed by model+version; manifest contains fragment id, placement list, fragment size, and preferred NCCL rings.

Activation-slicing flow (per request):
1) The router assigns a request to a serving pod and computes the slice plan based on sequence length, model manifest, and SLO.
2) If the plan contains "local-only" fragments (fully present locally), process up to S tokens of the sequence without cross-GPU collectives.
3) For steps that require non-local fragments, do a fixed-size gather window: fetch the needed fragments async using RDMA/peer-to-peer and apply those tokens as a mini-batch.
4) Local KV updates are buffered and pushed to replicas asynchronously with epoch stamps. Remote reconciliation uses versioned ops to converge (no strong consistency required for inference).

Rationale: many user sequences have early prefixes that are short or localizable; slicing allows serving those cheaply. Bulk of the long-tail work is handled via higher-latency fetches but amortized across S tokens, keeping per-token latency bounded.

NCCL and collective strategy:
- Topology detection: on pod startup, run a topology probe to detect PCIe/IB/ethernet links and create ring groups. Store ring group ids in manifest.
- For intra-rack, prefer ring-based all-gather with chunking tuned to NIC MTU and GPU PCIe lanes. For cross-rack, prefer hierarchical tree collectives (reduce-scatter + all-gather) to reduce cross-rack bandwidth spikes.
- Chunking heuristic: chunk_size = max(1MB, bandwidth_estimate * target_token_time * 0.7). Adjust per-request based on observed per-chunk latency.
- Adaptive collective fallback: if p99(nccl_latency) exceeds threshold or network errors observed, switch the request to the "pipeline-stitch" mode (see below) for the next N tokens.

Pipeline / tensor parallel mapping:
- Tensor-parallel groups keep weights sharded across members; fragments are aligned with tensor shards where possible to avoid additional scatter/gather.
- Pipeline stages map to fragments when model supports layer partitioning. We prefer layer-granular pipeline cuts (coarse-grained) to minimize inter-stage handoff overhead.
- When activation-slicing overlaps pipeline stage boundaries, use double-buffered handoff: while stage k processes slice t+1, stage k+1 completes slice t and can prefetch the next fragment set. This enables overlap of compute and communication.

Microbatching and batching policy:
- Microbatch size interacts with slice size. We define two knobs: slice_tokens and microbatch_count. The effective latency is slice_tokens / (tokens/sec) + NCCL overhead per reconciliation.
- Default initial config: slice_tokens=8, microbatch_count=4 for interactive routes; slice_tokens=128, microbatch_count=32 for throughput routes. These are tuned per-model.

Consistency model and correctness:
- KV entries annotated with "epoch" and "source" so replicas can accept idempotent updates. The serving runtime tolerates stale remote fragments for up to X seconds (configurable per route).
- If a request must have deterministic outputs for audit, the router can pin the request to a fully replicated pod or use synchronous fetch mode (higher latency).

Failure and degraded modes:
- Network congestion: switch to pipeline-stitch mode where we route tokens through a single replica that holds the required fragments; this trades CPU/GPU for network.
- Node OOM: evict cold fragments (LRU by last-accessed + request-affinity boost) and, if necessary, fall back to synchronous cross-pod fetches for cold entries.
- Collective failure: mark ring group as degraded and notify scheduler to avoid packing new requests that rely on that group until repair.

Observability and metrics:
- New metrics: fragment_hit_rate, fragment_fetch_ms(p50/p95/p99), slice_processing_ms, nccl_chunk_ms, reconcile_lag_seconds.
- Logs should include per-request slice plan and which fragments were local vs remote, plus NCCL ring chosen and any fallback transitions.

Experiments to run (short list):
1) Microbenchmark: synthetic model with configurable KV size; measure p50/p95 token latency with slice_tokens in {1,4,8,16,32} and varying replication factors.
2) Topology-aware collectives: run same workload with ring-only, tree-only, and hybrid; measure tail latency and cross-rack egress.
3) Real workload replay: take 72h of production traces and simulate routing policies to estimate fragment hotness and required memory footprint for different shard granularities.

Implementation roadmap (MVP -> v1 -> v2):
- MVP (6 weeks): fragment manifest, local fragment placement, simple activation-slicing in pod (single-node only), basic metrics; no asynchronous reconciliation (sync fetch).
- v1 (12 weeks): async fragment fetch and buffered local updates, topology probe + simple ring grouping, rollback-safe metadata updates, basic degraded mode (pipeline-stitch).
- v2 (Q3): hierarchical collectives, per-tenant placement policies, automated placement optimizer (cost model), stronger replica consistency options, integration with Console rollouts and Optimize suggestions.

Open questions / risks:
- Optimal fragment granularity: small fragments reduce fetch volume but increase metadata and fetch overhead. Need experiments to find sweet spot per model size/fleet.
- Memory amplification from replication vs NCCL overhead: what's the break-even point for replication across rack vs fetch-on-demand?
- Debuggability: complex async reconciliation increases surface area for subtle consistency bugs; need deterministic test harness.

Action items (owners):
- Run trace replay to generate hotness heatmaps for 124B and 13B models (Ethan).
- Prototype single-pod activation-slicing shim, include metrics (Samir).
- Write topology probing PoC and store ring groups in metadata service (Lina).
- Add fragment manifest schema draft to repo (Maya).

Appendix: example slice plan (informal)
- Request: seq_len=2048, route=SLA-interactive
- Plan: [local_only: first 256 tokens], [slice: 8 tokens x 4 microbatches], [remote_sync_fetch: layers 24-40 fragments], [fallback_threshold: 2x baseline_nccl_ms] -> use pipeline-stitch if exceeded.

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus feedback on the trade-offs between replication cost and slice size.
- Any prior notes/PRs that touch fragment placement or NCCL tuning, call them out in replies so we can unify heuristics.

End.
